title: Software Architecture as Trade-offs — Boundaries, Coupling, Consistency, Evolution

authoring_notes.purpose: Application/codebase-design-altitude software architecture taught as a single connected argument rather than a pattern catalogue. The course teaches how to choose and reason about monolith vs modular-monolith vs microservices, DDD (strategic + tactical), hexagonal/clean architecture, service decomposition and topology, API/integration contracts, data and consistency across boundaries, resilience patterns, and architectural evolution — always at the trade-off altitude (why/when each pattern, and what it costs). It is NOT an infrastructure or distributed-systems-internals course (no Raft/Paxos, Kafka internals, k8s) and NOT an ML/model-architecture course; consistency and resilience appear only at the design-decision altitude. Source library: wiki/raw-data/software-arch/ (21 web-quoted + book-thesis excerpts, crawl-assembled; no local clone).
authoring_notes.framing: This is a DESIGN-DECISION course, not an implementation course. The unit of study is the architectural decision and its reversal cost, not a codebase or a model. The course spine is one idea, stated in [[insights]]: architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to reverse; every pattern is a bet about which changes you keep cheap; everything is a trade-off — if you can't name the cost, you haven't understood the pattern (the First Law, quoted in [[richards-ford-fundamentals]]). The four pillars from [[insights]] — Boundaries, Coupling & Cohesion, Consistency & Events, Evolution & Decisions — are the structural backbone.
authoring_notes.why_this_learner: UC Berkeley EECS; research-framing-priority; already thinks natively in trade-offs (so present every pattern as a priced bet, never as a best practice — lean on the First Law and 'no best practices' from [[richards-ford-hard-parts]]). Skip math scaffolding. Wants the core insight + real primary-source quotes, not paraphrase. Building a production sales agent (Lina TMR) over many external SaaS tools, and recently closed an agent-benchmark course (automation-bench) — so the research-framing payoff here is designing the agent's architecture, not evaluating it. Every chapter should connect at least one pattern back to that system, and the final lab makes the whole toolkit produce a real design memo for it. The through-line is pre-named in [[insights]]: every external SaaS API response is 'outside data' ([[helland-data-outside-inside]]); the agent should default to a modular monolith with clean bounded contexts and extract a service only when granularity disintegrators clearly win.
authoring_notes.structure: 10 chapters in 6 phases following the four-pillar progression. foundations (ch-01) installs the spine and the decision/communication tools. boundaries (ch-02..ch-03): strategic DDD / bounded contexts, then structure-inside-a-boundary (hexagonal + clean + tactical DDD merged). topology (ch-04): monolith vs modular-monolith vs microservices, decompose-by-capability, Conway/Team Topologies, the architecture quantum, the distributed-monolith trap. contracts (ch-05): REST/RMM/API styles, versioning/idempotency, consumer-driven contracts. consistency (ch-06..ch-07): inside-vs-outside data + sagas + outbox as the core, then CQRS/event-sourcing as optional power tools layered on top. evolution (ch-08..ch-09): resilience/stability patterns + observability as architecture, then strangler-fig migration + fitness functions + evolutionary architecture. capstone (ch-10): a LAB applying the whole toolkit to the learner's real sales agent. Dependencies are strictly sequential and honest; no chapter depends on a later one.
authoring_notes.per_chapter_format: Each read.md must (1) QUOTE the real primary sources via [[excerpt-slug]] wikilinks — the excerpts already carry verbatim quotes from the free articles (Fowler, Cockburn mirror, Martin, Young/Fowler, Richardson, Fielding's gbiv.com mirror, Robinson, Nygard's ADR post, Brown) and clearly-marked book theses (Evans, Vernon, Newman, Richards/Ford x2, Nygard Release It!, Skelton & Pais, Helland); reproduce the quote with attribution exactly as the excerpt records it, never paraphrasing book theses as if verbatim; (2) extract the chapter's Core Insight + one practitioner Guideline (the excerpt headers seed both); (3) surface the relevant doc-vs-reality myth from the reconciliation table in [[COLLECTION-PLAN]] and resolve it with the primary source; (4) price the pattern as a bet — name explicitly what it keeps cheap to change and what it makes expensive; (5) connect at least one move back to the learner's sales-agent system. Chapters may emit self-contained companion HTML under ch-XX/figures/ (inline CSS/JS, no CDNs) for things markdown handles poorly: a C4 zoom explorer, a dependency-rule / hexagon diagram, a saga choreography-vs-orchestration animation, a circuit-breaker state machine, an inside-vs-outside data flow, a granularity disintegrators-vs-integrators balance, a strangler-fig migration timeline. HTML amplifies; markdown + wikilinks stays the backbone.
authoring_notes.depth_target: Source-rich. Every mechanism claim is backed by a quoted primary source or a clearly-marked book thesis from the excerpts, not paraphrase. Where the popular narrative and the primary source disagree, the primary source wins and the gap is named (the 10-row reconciliation table in [[COLLECTION-PLAN]] is the canonical myth list). Honor the gap log: Cockburn .us cert / Fielding ics.uci cert / Helland Queue 403 / Sagas-1987 image-only PDF are corroborated via mirrors/summaries and must be cited as such, not as clean fetches.
authoring_notes.tradeoff_spine_notes: The trade-off spine threads through every chapter as a fixed move: each pattern is introduced, then immediately priced as a bet — 'this keeps X cheap to change at the cost of making Y expensive.' ch-01 installs the First Law ([[richards-ford-fundamentals]]) and the 'architecture = hard-to-change decisions' definition so the spine has vocabulary. Boundaries (ch-02..04) are framed as the most expensive-to-reverse decision, which is exactly why the course defers them (modular-monolith-first via [[fowler-monolith-first]]). Contracts (ch-05) are framed as the most expensive-to-reverse artifact a service owns. Consistency (ch-06..07) prices the cost of crossing a boundary: loss of locks and shared transactions ([[helland-data-outside-inside]]), loss of isolation in sagas ([[richardson-saga]]), 'risky complexity' for CQRS/ES ([[young-cqrs-es]]). Evolution (ch-08..09) is about keeping the bet revisable: stability patterns bound the blast radius, fitness functions stop the chosen characteristics from rotting, strangler-fig makes migration itself reversible. The lab forces the learner to make every bet explicit in an ADR + C4 sketch for their own system. The over-arching myth the spine kills: 'microservices/DDD/CQRS/REST are best practices' — none are; each is a trade with a named cost ([[richards-ford-hard-parts]]: 'no best practices').
authoring_notes.reconciliation_myths_by_chapter: ch-01: 'a C4 container is a Docker container' (false; [[c4-model]]) + 'architecture = best practices' (no; First Law). ch-02: 'DDD requires microservices' (false; DDD is a modeling discipline, contexts can be modules; [[ddd-bounded-context]]). ch-04: 'microservices are the modern best practice / monoliths are legacy' (no; MonolithFirst + MicroservicePremium; [[fowler-monolith-first]], [[fowler-microservices]]) + 'split and get loose coupling for free' (no; distributed monolith; [[distributed-monolith]]) + 'pick service size by a rule of thumb' (no; disintegrators-vs-integrators; [[richards-ford-hard-parts]]) + 'Conway's Law is folklore' (no; Inverse Conway Maneuver; [[conway-team-topologies]]). ch-05: 'our API is RESTful' (most are Level-2 HTTP-RPC; level 3 hypermedia is a precondition of REST per Fielding/Fowler; [[fielding-rest]]). ch-06: 'use 2PC across services' (no; services don't share transactions; sagas + outbox; [[helland-data-outside-inside]], [[richardson-saga]], [[transactional-outbox]]) + 'eventual consistency is an infra problem' (no; it's an app-design problem; [[fowler-microservices]], [[helland-data-outside-inside]]). ch-07: 'CQRS and Event Sourcing are the same thing / go together' (no; independent, composable, each adds risky complexity; [[young-cqrs-es]]).
authoring_notes.merge_split_decisions: Two deliberate merges vs the suggested 9-step progression, both grounded in the excerpts themselves. (1) Hexagonal + Clean + tactical-DDD/aggregates are ONE chapter (ch-03): [[cockburn-hexagonal]] and [[martin-clean-arch]] state outright they are 'the same idea, three names' (technology-free core, inward dependencies, I/O at the edges), and [[ddd-aggregates-tactical]] is the in-process consistency seed that belongs with structure-inside-a-boundary (its aggregate rule 4 is the in-process seed of the later distributed saga). (2) CQRS/Event-Sourcing shares the consistency arc but gets its OWN chapter (ch-07) layered after the inside/outside-data + saga + outbox core (ch-06), because [[young-cqrs-es]]'s load-bearing teaching is that they are OPTIONAL power tools scoped to a portion of the system — keeping them separate from the mandatory consistency mechanics prevents the conflation the reconciliation table warns against. Net effect: the suggested 9 content steps + lab compress cleanly into 10 chapters.

tracks.title: The Spine: Decisions, Trade-offs, and the Tools to Record Them
Boundaries: Where to Cut and How to Structure Inside the Cut
Decomposition & Topology: Monolith, Modular Monolith, Microservices
Integration Contracts: API Styles and Safe Evolution
Crossing the Boundary: Data, Consistency, and Events
Resilience & Evolution: Keeping the Bet Revisable
Capstone Lab: Architecting the Production Sales Agent

chapters.title: Architecture Is the Expensive-to-Reverse Decisions
concepts: The spine, installed: 'architecture is the stuff that's hard to change' / the deep binding decisions, and every pattern downstream is a bet about which changes you keep cheap ([[richards-ford-fundamentals]], [[insights]])

The First Law as the course's organizing principle: 'Everything in software architecture is a trade-off… if you think you've found something that isn't, you likely just haven't found the trade-off yet' — and the corollary 'no best practices' ([[richards-ford-fundamentals]], [[richards-ford-hard-parts]])

Architecture characteristics (the '-ilities'): derive the critical few from requirements rather than maximizing all — deployability pushes toward services, simplicity pushes back to a monolith ([[richards-ford-fundamentals]])
ADRs as the durable record of the why: Title/Status/Context/Decision/Consequences, 'a conversation with a future developer,' for 'architecturally significant' decisions ([[nygard-release-it]])

C4 as the shared notation at one zoom level (Context -> Container -> Component -> Code); myth killed: a C4 'container' is any separately deployable app or data store, NOT a Docker container ([[c4-model]], [[COLLECTION-PLAN]])
Framing the whole course for the learner's sales agent: which of its decisions are the expensive-to-reverse ones, and Fowler's amendment that a good architect shrinks the irreversible set

chapters.title: Boundaries by Language: Strategic DDD and Bounded Contexts
concepts: Why one unified model fails: 'Total unification of the domain model for a large system will not be feasible or cost-effective' — split where the language changes ([[ddd-bounded-context]])

Bounded Context + Ubiquitous Language: an explicit boundary inside which one model holds without contradiction; the polysemy signal ('Customer' means a pipeline lead in Sales, an account-with-tickets in Support) ([[ddd-bounded-context]])

Context mapping between contexts — Partnership, Shared Kernel, Customer-Supplier, Conformist, Anticorruption Layer, Open Host Service, Published Language — as strategic decisions with org consequences ([[ddd-bounded-context]])

Myth killed: 'DDD requires microservices' is false; DDD is a modeling discipline and bounded contexts can be modules inside a modular monolith — no DDD source ties it to a deployment topology ([[ddd-bounded-context]], [[COLLECTION-PLAN]])
Pricing the bet: a bounded context drawn on the slowest-changing structure (language/domain) is the boundary worth committing to; a wrong one is a model rot you pay for daily
Applied to the sales agent: finding the bounded contexts (e.g. lead/pipeline vs conversation vs scheduling vs CRM-sync) before deciding anything about deployment

chapters.title: Structure Inside a Boundary: Hexagonal, Clean, and Aggregates
concepts: The Dependency Rule as the whole architecture in one sentence: 'Source code dependencies can only point inwards' — policy never depends on detail; cross boundaries with plain DTOs, not ORM rows or framework objects ([[martin-clean-arch]])

Hexagonal / Ports & Adapters: 'Allow an application to equally be driven by users, programs, automated test or batch scripts… in isolation from its eventual run-time devices and databases'; primary/driving vs secondary/driven adapters; the hexagon's six sides are incidental ([[cockburn-hexagonal]])

Same idea, three names: Clean = Hexagonal = Onion (technology-free core, inward dependencies, I/O at the edges via interfaces the core owns) — Clean states the rule, Hexagonal gives the testability motivation ([[martin-clean-arch]], [[cockburn-hexagonal]])
Tactical DDD inside the core: entity vs value object vs aggregate vs domain event; the aggregate is the unit of immediate transactional consistency ([[ddd-aggregates-tactical]])

Vernon's four aggregate rules: model true invariants in consistency boundaries; design small aggregates; reference other aggregates by identity; use eventual consistency outside the boundary — rule 4 is the in-process seed of the distributed saga ([[ddd-aggregates-tactical]])

Pricing the bet: indirection/boilerplate (ports, DTOs, mappers) is overkill for small CRUD but exactly right for the learner's long-lived agent core, insulating domain policy from whichever LLM API / vector DB / framework is current ([[martin-clean-arch]])

chapters.title: Monolith, Modular Monolith, Microservices, and the Quantum
concepts: Microservices defined by independent deployability (not size): the 9 characteristics and the explicit benefit/cost table, with the authors' own hedge 'we write this with cautious optimism' and the MicroservicePremium ([[fowler-microservices]], [[newman-building-microservices]])

MonolithFirst + the modular monolith middle ground: 'Almost all the successful microservice stories have started with a monolith'; a bad boundary inside a monolith is a refactor, across services it's a migration ([[fowler-monolith-first]])

Decompose by business capability / subdomain (the two converge): cut on the slowest-changing structure for a 'stable architecture'; reject layer-based splits that guarantee coupling ([[decompose-by-business-capability]])

Conway's Law and the socio-technical boundary: 'any organization… will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure'; the Inverse Conway Maneuver; Team Topologies' four team types and cognitive load as the real constraint ([[conway-team-topologies]])

The architecture quantum as the boundary test (smallest independently-deployable, cohesive unit with its OWN data) + granularity disintegrators vs integrators — size is the OUTPUT of trade-off analysis, not a rule of thumb ([[richards-ford-hard-parts]])

Myths killed + the distributed-monolith trap: 'microservices are best practice / monoliths are legacy' and 'split and get loose coupling for free' — services that deploy together or share a DB are 'all the pain of distributed systems without the independence' ([[distributed-monolith]], [[COLLECTION-PLAN]])

chapters.title: Integration Contracts: REST, API Styles, and Safe Evolution
concepts: REST as a set of constraints (client-server, stateless, cache, uniform interface, layered, optional code-on-demand) chosen to buy web-scale evolvability — quoted from Fielding's gbiv.com mirror (ics.uci cert was broken; cite the mirror) ([[fielding-rest]], [[COLLECTION-PLAN]])

Richardson Maturity Model (Level 0 'Swamp of POX' -> resources -> verbs -> hypermedia) and the myth killed: 'our API is RESTful' — most are Level-2 HTTP-RPC; Fielding made clear level 3 hypermedia is a precondition of REST ([[fielding-rest]], [[COLLECTION-PLAN]])

API-style selection as a trade-off: REST/HTTP for cacheable evolvable resources, gRPC for low-latency internal service-to-service, GraphQL for client-driven aggregation — pick by the property you need ([[fielding-rest]])

Versioning and idempotency: prefer additive backward/forward-compatible change over versioned breakage; make writes idempotent (idempotency keys) so retries are safe under at-least-once delivery ([[fielding-rest]], [[transactional-outbox]])

Consumer-Driven Contracts + tolerant reader ('conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept'); the consumer publishes a pact, the provider runs it in CI — the only mechanism that preserves independent deployability ([[consumer-driven-contracts]], [[newman-building-microservices]])

Pricing the bet: the published contract is the most expensive-to-reverse artifact a service owns — breaking it costs coordinated multi-team migration; applied to the agent's tool/integration layer over many SaaS APIs ([[consumer-driven-contracts]], [[richards-ford-hard-parts]])

chapters.title: Inside vs Outside Data: Sagas and the Transactional Outbox
concepts: Helland's root distinction: inside data (private, mutable, ACID, 'now') vs outside data (immutable, versioned, identity-stamped, possibly stale) — the moment data crosses a boundary you lose locks and shared transactions ([[helland-data-outside-inside]])

The three load-bearing claims: services don't share transactions; outside data must be immutable (safe to retry/cache/replay); outside data may be stale, so design for eventual consistency at app altitude ([[helland-data-outside-inside]])

Myths killed: 'use 2PC across services' (services don't share transactions; 2PC across DB+broker not viable) and 'eventual consistency is an infra problem' (it's a design problem — 'business logic can end up making decisions on inconsistent information') ([[helland-data-outside-inside]], [[fowler-microservices]], [[COLLECTION-PLAN]])

Database per Service + the dual-write problem; the Saga as a sequence of local transactions glued by events with compensating transactions (Garcia-Molina 1987 LLT origin — image-only PDF, thesis-extracted); choreography vs orchestration ([[richardson-saga]], [[transactional-outbox]])

The price of a saga: loss of isolation (the 'I' in ACID) and the required countermeasures (semantic locks, commutative updates, re-reads, by-value tracking) — a saga is not a free transaction ([[richardson-saga]])

Transactional Outbox: persist the event in the same local transaction, relay asynchronously (polling publisher vs CDC log-tailing), consumers must be idempotent under at-least-once delivery; applied to every external SaaS response in the agent as outside data ([[transactional-outbox]], [[helland-data-outside-inside]])

chapters.title: CQRS and Event Sourcing: Optional Power Tools
concepts: CQRS defined: 'use a different model to update information than the model you use to read information' (Greg Young, via Fowler) — and scope it tightly ([[young-cqrs-es]])

The load-bearing caution: 'for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity'; 'CQRS should only be used on specific portions of a system… not the system as a whole'; 'many systems do fit a CRUD mental model' ([[young-cqrs-es]])

Event Sourcing defined: 'capture all changes to an application state as a sequence of events'; rebuild state by replaying the log; benefits = audit log, temporal queries, replay debugging ([[young-cqrs-es]])
Event Sourcing's sharp edges and caution: 'don't go down this path unless you really need to' — external side-effects on replay, historical-event schema evolution ([[young-cqrs-es]])

Myth killed: 'CQRS and Event Sourcing are the same / go together' — they are independent decisions that compose; neither requires the other, and neither requires microservices ([[young-cqrs-es]], [[COLLECTION-PLAN]])

Pricing the bet + the seed: both are bets you refuse unless a specific force (asymmetric read/write scaling, true audit/replay need) demands them; the in-process seed is the aggregate emitting domain events ([[ddd-aggregates-tactical]], [[young-cqrs-es]])

chapters.title: Resilience as Architecture: Stability at the Integration Points
concepts: Cascading Failure as the motivating anti-pattern: every integration point is where failure enters and spreads; 'Integration Points without Timeouts is a surefire way to create Cascading Failures' ([[nygard-release-it]])

The stability toolkit: Timeout (bound every remote wait), Circuit Breaker (open and fail fast over a dead dependency, half-open to test recovery), Bulkhead (partition pools like a ship's hull), Steady State, Fail Fast ([[nygard-release-it]])

Why this is design altitude, not ops: where you place breakers and bulkheads defines the blast radius; a distributed monolith is precisely the system that skipped them ([[nygard-release-it]], [[distributed-monolith]])

Async/event integration as itself a resilience decision: choosing events over synchronous chains removes the coupling these patterns otherwise have to defend ([[nygard-release-it]], [[richardson-saga]])

Observability and characteristics-monitoring at design altitude: deciding what must be observable is an architectural choice tied to the critical architecture characteristics ([[richards-ford-fundamentals]], [[nygard-release-it]])
Applied to the agent: every external SaaS call is an integration point needing a timeout + circuit breaker + bulkhead so one slow/down vendor can't stall the whole agent loop

chapters.title: Evolution: Strangler-Fig Migration and Fitness Functions
concepts: Why big-bang rewrites fail: 'Replacing a serious IT system takes a long time, and the users can't wait'; the strangler-fig grows the new system around the old and retires it piece by piece ([[martin-strangler-fig]])

The strangler mechanism at design altitude: intercept via façade/proxy -> extract one capability seam -> verify & shrink -> repeat; 'investment and returns occur gradually and visibly' with low per-step risk ([[martin-strangler-fig]])

Strangler-fig as reversibility discipline + Newman's incremental playbook: extract behavior AND its data together to avoid a shared-DB dependency mid-migration; the operational counterpart to MonolithFirst ([[martin-strangler-fig]], [[newman-building-microservices]], [[fowler-monolith-first]])
Evolutionary architecture: 'supports guided, incremental change across multiple dimensions' — keeping the bet revisable rather than frozen ([[richards-ford-fundamentals]])

Fitness functions: 'an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristic(s)' — an automated check (test/metric/monitor/ArchUnit rule) that fails the build when a protected characteristic erodes; turns 'keep the dependency rule' or 'p99 < X' from aspiration into enforcement ([[richards-ford-fundamentals]], [[martin-clean-arch]])

Pricing the bet: evolution costs ongoing enforcement and migration discipline, but it is how the expensive-to-reverse decisions are kept from rotting silently; deciding which agent seam to strangle first

chapters.title: Lab: Architecting the Production Sales Agent (ADR + C4)
concepts: Identify the bounded contexts of the sales agent (Lina TMR) and where the ubiquitous language changes across lead/pipeline, conversation, scheduling, and CRM-sync ([[ddd-bounded-context]], [[decompose-by-business-capability]])

Default to a modular-monolith-first topology with clean internal boundaries; run the architecture-quantum + disintegrators-vs-integrators analysis to decide which seam (if any) to extract and when ([[fowler-monolith-first]], [[richards-ford-hard-parts]], [[distributed-monolith]])

Apply inside/outside-data discipline to every external SaaS API response: treat each as an immutable, versioned, possibly-stale snapshot, never as authoritative live state; separate the agent's inside model from what it ingests/emits ([[helland-data-outside-inside]], [[transactional-outbox]])

Design the contracts for the tool/integration layer (style selection, additive versioning, idempotency, consumer-driven contracts) and the resilience at every integration point (timeout/circuit breaker/bulkhead) ([[consumer-driven-contracts]], [[fielding-rest]], [[nygard-release-it]])

Make every choice a priced bet recorded as an ADR (Context/Decision/Consequences) and produce a C4 Context + Container sketch where a distributed monolith would become visible ([[nygard-release-it]], [[c4-model]], [[richards-ford-fundamentals]])

Deliverable: an ADR-style design memo + a C4 Context/Container sketch for the production sales agent — the research-framing payoff (previously built an agent benchmark; now design the agent's architecture)
